chapter_title: LangGraph in Depth: Building Durable Agent Graphs
audit: The dispatch-office analogy explains parallel reports but does not show how an immutable evidence reducer treats retransmission and contradiction. Lesson A follows the same fields across three merges: a new entry is accepted, an identical repeated entry adds nothing, and a conflicting value under the same ID is rejected. Lesson B narrows the commander policy to the two highest risk classes and draws every approval outcome. Readers can see why two valid approvers matter for risk 4 and why approval cannot unlock risk 5. These focused views complement the existing graph diagrams without implying that a route annotation creates authority or a checkpoint rewinds external effects.

lessons.title: Retransmission is not new evidence
lessons.intro: Two AegisOps branches return evidence E-17. The reducer treats each evidence identity as immutable, so identical retransmission and conflicting content must behave differently.

data.invariant: An accepted evidence ID never silently changes its content.

read: The second arrival does not increase the ledger size.
The conflicting third update cannot replace E-17.
A genuine correction needs a new version with a supersession link.
lessons.question: If the child subgraph returns its received E-17 plus E-17 again, how many entries should remain?
lessons.answer: One under this immutable-ID reducer, provided both copies have identical content. A simple append reducer would preserve duplicates. If the contents differ under E-17, reject the merge rather than choosing whichever branch finishes last. Presentation order should be separate from evidential priority.
lessons.takeaway: Define merge semantics from evidence meaning before parallelizing nodes.
lessons.assumption: Fictional state; the reducer is atomic for each merge. The shown merge outcome is explanatory instrumentation.

lessons.anchor: Build it: the AegisOps commander as a LangGraph graph
lessons.title: Two high-risk branches, four explicit outcomes
lessons.intro: Inspect only proposals classified as risk 4 or risk 5 by deterministic AegisOps policy. Lower risk classes are outside this deliberately narrow tree.
read: The risk classification comes from policy, not model confidence.
Risk 4 approval clears only the approval gate.
Both risk 5 leaves block execution, including the approved-looking case.
lessons.question: Can a runbook entry or two approvers turn a risk 5 proposal into an executable action?
lessons.answer: No. This blueprint blocks that action class. The risk 3 runbook exception does not extend to risks 4 or 5. A different allowed proposal requires its own identity, classification and authority; editing the old proposal cannot inherit an earlier approval.
lessons.takeaway: Approval satisfies a permitted gate; it cannot override a blocked action class.
lessons.assumption: Fictional policy examples restricted to risks 4 and 5; valid approval includes binding, roles, expiry and consumption checks.
